mission.title: About this guide
mission.text: We want every traveller to Kanchanaburi to understand the River Kwai Bridge before they arrive — how a wartime railway became a place of memory. We gathered scattered official information, local stories and practical tips into one calm, ad-free guide, so a visit becomes a real encounter with history.

sunsetPlanner.title: Sunset & blue hour
sunsetPlanner.note: Arrive about 60 minutes before sunset. Roughly 30 minutes after sunset the bridge and riverside glow — prime time for photos. The blue hour (about 20–30 min after sunset) frames sky and steel together, most photogenic.
sunsetPlanner.seaGlare: Lighting tip: the bridge is most photogenic in the soft light just before and after sunset; midday is harsh and busy.
sunsetPlanner.tideTip: Crowd tip: early morning and the hour before sunset are calmest; midday is hottest and busiest.

intro.title: Meet the River Kwai Bridge
intro.description: The River Kwai Bridge is part of the Burma–Thailand (Death) Railway, built by Imperial Japan between 1942 and 1943 to link Thailand with Burma. Constructed under brutal conditions by Allied prisoners of war and tens of thousands of Asian forced labourers, the line became known for the enormous human cost of its construction. The bridge you see today is a reconstruction: parts were destroyed in Allied bombing and rebuilt after the war. Trains still run across it, and the riverbanks have become a place where history, daily life, and remembrance meet.

transportSection.title: How to get to the River Kwai Bridge
transportSection.subtitle: The easiest ways from Bangkok and beyond — pick what fits.
transportSection.overviewText: The bridge sits on River Kwai Road in Tha Ma Kham, on the south bank of the Khwae Yai, about 3 km from central Kanchanaburi. It is roughly a 2–3 hour drive west of Bangkok.
transportSection.overviewText2: Kanchanaburi is also reachable by train and bus; once in town, the bridge is a short taxi or songthaew ride away.

bestTime.title: Best season to visit
bestTime.text: Cool season (Nov–Feb) is most pleasant for walking the bridge. Hot season (Mar–May) is very warm — go after 16:00. Rainy season (Jun–Oct) brings showers; the river is fullest and the hills greenest.

officialManagement.title: Management & public order
officialManagement.text: The bridge sits at the meeting point of railway, tourism, and local community. The State Railway of Thailand operates the active line, the Tourism Authority of Thailand promotes the site, and Kanchanaburi Province manages local infrastructure and the annual River Kwai Bridge Week. Riverside vendors and museums keep the area welcoming. Please follow on-site guidance and visit respectfully.

humanities.title: The bridge: then and now
humanities.subtitle: From a wartime strategic line to a symbol remembered around the world.

sections.title: Forced Construction
sections.content: The Japanese Empire mobilized around 60,000 Allied POWs and hundreds of thousands of Asian forced laborers (Romusha), building it under brutal conditions with immense loss of life.

sections.title: Allied Bombing
sections.content: As a strategic chokepoint, the middle spans of the bridge were precisely destroyed by Allied air raids on several occasions.

sections.title: Restoration & Rebirth
sections.content: Fully repaired by the Thai government after the war, it continues to carry daily trains today and has become a pilgrimage site for peace-lovers worldwide.

didYouKnow.title: Movie Fiction vs. Reality
didYouKnow.text: Pierre Boulle's novel and the 1957 Oscar-winning film 'The Bridge on the River Kwai' made it globally famous, but many movie scenes were shot in Sri Lanka, and the true history is far more brutal than the cinematic portrayal. The real story of the Death Railway carries a much heavier weight than what the silver screen shows.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.subtitle: The most-asked things about the River Kwai Bridge.

items.a: The bridge and riverside are accessible around the clock; trains run on a daytime schedule, so plan around them.
No — walking across the bridge is free. Nearby museums may charge a small fee.
Mornings and the hour before sunset are coolest and best lit; midday is hot and busy.
It is part of the WWII Death Railway, built by POWs and forced labourers; the 1957 film fixed its name in global memory.

items.q: Can you still ride a train across?
items.a: Yes — the State Railway of Thailand runs passenger services on the line.

items.q: What happened to the original bridge?
items.a: Parts were destroyed in wartime bombing and rebuilt after the war; it still carries trains.
Train or bus to Kanchanaburi (2–3 hrs), then a short taxi or songthaew to the bridge.

items.q: Hard to get a ride back?
items.a: Pre-book Grab/Bolt, or walk to the main road for a songthaew; off-peak is easier.
About 3 km from central Kanchanaburi; a few minutes by songthaew.

items.q: Is the bridge walkway wheelchair / stroller friendly?
items.a: Partly. The walkway runs on open sleepers with gaps between them and no side barriers, so wheelchairs and strollers need care; the north-bank riverside promenade is level and easier for those who need it.
Yes, with supervision — keep children close, mind the gaps between sleepers and the open sides, and step aside well before a train passes.

items.q: Any walking cautions on the bridge?
items.a: Wear closed shoes; heels can catch in the sleeper gaps, and the sides are open with no rail — don't lean or climb over. Step aside for trains.
